task_brief: Day 5 of "Music Theory, Notation, and Analytical Listening" (unit 2, grade 9) is a second concept model on ear training and transcription. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Transcribe and analyse a public-domain or original passage, documenting harmonic function and an ear-training growth record. Today's work contributes to that by handling ear training and transcription at the concept model b stage, against the unit's wider topics of key signatures and modal scales, intervals triads and seventh chords, rhythm meter and syncopation, and score reading and analysis of public-domain works. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Study a second, contrasting model work for ear training and transcription and set it beside the first one you examined earlier in this unit. Build a comparison naming one choice the two makers share and one place they clearly diverge, with the effect of each difference described in terms a listener or viewer could verify. Then make one short study of your own that borrows the second maker's approach to ear training and transcription. Cite both works. Anything you did not make yourself must be public domain, openly licensed, or properly attributed. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about ear training and transcription, and it belongs to "Music Theory, Notation, and Analytical Listening", which also covers separate topics such as key signatures and modal scales. Close out with this check before you stop: State what the contrasting example of ear training and transcription revealed that the first one did not. At grade 9 the bar is independent work with explicit criteria set before you start, and evidence that you evaluated the finished result against those criteria rather than against how it felt.
requirements: Meet this lesson's own success criteria: The learner completes the central task on ear training and transcription., The learner supplies evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer., and The learner checks or revises the work and can name a next step.

Produce the deliverable for a second concept model: Two-work comparison naming a shared choice and a divergence, one short study in the second approach, and citations for both works.
Show the process, not only the result — a working log, draft, or annotated study.
Complete the critique criteria list in this package before submitting.
deliverable: Two-work comparison naming a shared choice and a divergence, one short study in the second approach, and citations for both works.
critique_criteria: One shared choice and one clear divergence between the two model works are both named.
The effect of each difference is described in verifiable terms rather than as preference.
A short original study borrows the second work's approach.
Both works are cited; nothing uncredited and nothing outside public-domain or licensed use appears.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available and scores the same. Instead of performing, speaking, or recording, you may submit a written description of what you made or would make, a notated or diagrammed version, a labelled plan, or a written analysis covering the same criteria. Nothing in this task requires a working microphone, camera, or the ability to perform aloud.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.

Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, notated, constructed, or demonstrated responses. Where performance is the target, a private demonstration to one trusted adult carries the same weight as any audience, and requires no recording.
Provide adaptive instruments and grips, enlarged or braille notation, seated and standing studio access, low-odour and low-dust material substitutes, and hearing protection on request.

Where documentation quality is itself the target, document the artwork alone with no person in frame, or have an adult verify the physical work directly. Neither route requires an image of the learner, and both preserve the documentation target rather than replacing it.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task centres an aural element (ear training and transcription). Provide a fully equivalent non-aural route: notated, written, or graphic representation; visual or tactile pulse (a moving marker, a tapped or felt beat); and vibration or sight-reading in place of listening. Do not require the learner to hear a pitch, interval, or timbre to demonstrate understanding of it.

Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Public performance is never required. A private, low-audience, or written-and-scored alternative always carries the same academic target.
No recording of the learner’s voice, no photograph, and no video is ever required; documentation may be written, notated, sketched, or adult-verified instead.
Use only original, public-domain, licensed, or family-approved works. Do not reproduce full copyrighted lyrics, sheet music, or other protected works without documented rights.
The tutor may explain technique, ask diagnostic questions, and critique work, but never silently completes graded creative work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting ear training and transcription.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for ear training and transcription follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for ear training and transcription, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to ear training and transcription works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of ear training and transcription, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking ear training and transcription mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply ear training and transcription under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on ear training and transcription rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
